summary: Barlaam of Calabria (c. 1290-1348 CE), also called Barlaam of Seminara, was a Greek-speaking scholar, monk, and philosopher from southern Italy who became the principal opponent of Gregory Palamas in the fourteenth-century hesychast controversy, attacking the Athonite monks' claim to a vision of the uncreated light and their psychosomatic method of prayer; condemned at the Constantinople synod of 1341, he returned to Italy, entered the Latin church, and was made bishop of Gerace. He also disputed the filioque with the Latins and taught Greek to Petrarch.
description:
Barlaam was born around 1290 at Seminara in Calabria, in the Greek-speaking, formerly Byzantine milieu of southern Italy, and became a monk and an accomplished scholar of Greek philosophy, mathematics, and astronomy. He moved to the Byzantine East, where he was active in Constantinople and Thessalonica, taught, and was initially engaged by the imperial court in the negotiations over union with the Latin church, writing against the Latin doctrine of the procession of the Holy Spirit (the filioque) and against Roman papal primacy. In the West he is also remembered as one of the figures through whom Greek letters reached the early Italian humanists: he gave Greek lessons to Petrarch, and through his pupil Leontius Pilatus his teaching reached the circle of Boccaccio.

Barlaam is known above all as the principal opponent of Gregory Palamas in the hesychast controversy of the 1330s and 1340s. According to the account of his Palamite opponents, on which the surviving picture of his position largely rests, Barlaam attacked the Athonite hesychast monks on two fronts. He is reported to have ridiculed their psychosomatic method of prayer, the bodily posture and breathing joined to the Jesus Prayer by which they sought to draw the mind into the heart, and to have denied that their claimed experience of the light of Mount Tabor was a vision of the uncreated God, treating it instead as either a created, sensory phenomenon or a delusion. Behind this, his opponents present him as holding a strongly apophatic and agnostic epistemology of God: that God in himself is unknowable and that no direct experience or demonstrative knowledge of the divine can be had in this life, so that the monks' claims to behold the uncreated light overreached what is possible. Palamas answered him in The Triads (In Defense of the Holy Hesychasts) and with the Hagioritic Tome, developing against him the distinction between the unknowable divine essence and the uncreated divine energies. Barlaam's positions here are recorded as reported by his opponents and are contested; the editor does not adjudicate the dispute.

Barlaam was condemned at a synod held at Constantinople in 1341. After this defeat he left the Byzantine East, returned to Italy, and entered the Latin (Roman Catholic) church; he was appointed bishop of Gerace in Calabria, and he died around 1348. In later Byzantine polemic 'Barlaamite' became a label for the anti-Palamite party, and the synods of 1347 and 1351 that affirmed Palamas's teaching also anathematized Barlaam and his followers. His own works include treatises on logic, ethics, astronomy, and the anti-Latin and, later, pro-Latin controversies; because they are little read and he is known chiefly through the writings of those who opposed him, his theology is difficult to reconstruct except as his opponents reported it.
editorial_notes:
Barlaam is documented here as the principal opponent of Gregory Palamas, mirroring the gregory-palamas entry from the other side of the same controversy (neutrality #2). The decisive editorial caution is that Barlaam's own theological works are proprietary, little edited, and little read, and that his positions in the hesychast controversy survive largely through the writings of his Palamite opponents. His attacks on the hesychasts (the ridicule of the psychosomatic method, the denial that the Taboric light is uncreated) and his reported apophatic/agnostic epistemology of God are therefore presented throughout as ATTRIBUTED, that is, as reported by the anti-Barlaam sources, and are not stated as settled fact or endorsed (neutrality #1, #2). The synod of 1341 condemning him, his return to the Latin church, and his appointment as bishop of Gerace are recorded as historical facts without the editor ruling either side of the theological dispute correct (neutrality #1), exactly as the palamas entry records the councils' affirmation of Palamas without endorsing the doctrine. Where the controversy is described, neither Palamas's essence/energies distinction nor Barlaam's reported apophaticism is adjudicated; the reader judges.

Birth and death years (c. 1290-1348 CE) are approximate and as standardly reported in the scholarship. Sourcing follows the three-lens model per neutrality #8, adapted to a figure known mainly through his opponents: (a) academic historians of doctrine (Meyendorff, A Study of Gregory Palamas, the standard scholarly monograph on the controversy, which treats Barlaam's role and positions; Robert E. Sinkewicz, whose critical work on Barlaam's own texts and their philosophical context is the leading study of Barlaam in his own right); (b) the primary corpus, present here only indirectly and attributed, above all Palamas, The Triads, in which Barlaam's positions are quoted and answered by his opponent, so this is a hostile primary witness, cited as such; (c) contemporary reception through the standard Orthodox and Byzantinist scholarship on the controversy. No encyclopedias, no tertiary or popular sources.

CONFIDENCE HONESTY: this entry is reviewed-only, not verified. Barlaam's own works were not read line by line (they are proprietary and, in his own voice, largely unedited and inaccessible), and his positions are reconstructed from his opponents; accordingly the primary-witness source (Palamas, The Triads) is cited as an attributed, hostile witness to Barlaam's views and the Meyendorff and Sinkewicz monographs are rated medium, verified to exist and be on-topic via publisher and journal records but not read line by line. No source here is rated high, precisely because the subject is known through his opponents rather than through an openly readable primary text in his own voice. Relation targets gregory-palamas, hesychasm, essence-energies-distinction, and eastern-orthodoxy exist in the dataset; filioque is a dangling forward reference, not yet a separate entry.

lifespan.note: c. 1290-1348 CE; born at Seminara in Calabria (southern Italy), active in Constantinople and Thessalonica, condemned at Constantinople in 1341, returned to Italy and the Latin church, appointed bishop of Gerace. Dates are approximate as standardly reported in the scholarship.

relations.note: Barlaam and Palamas were the two principals of the hesychast controversy; Barlaam attacked the hesychasts and Palamas answered him in The Triads. Barlaam's opposition is attributed to him as his position in the dispute, reported largely by his Palamite opponents, and is not adjudicated here. Mirror of the 'refuted' relation in the gregory-palamas entry, from the other side.

Per the account of his opponents, Barlaam attacked the Athonite hesychasts' psychosomatic method of prayer and their claim to behold the uncreated light of Mount Tabor; presented as his reported position, not endorsed, and the controversy is not adjudicated.

Barlaam's attack on the hesychasts' claim to experience the uncreated light provoked, and was answered by, Palamas's distinction between the unknowable divine essence and the uncreated divine energies; Barlaam's reported apophatic/agnostic epistemology of God stands opposed to it. Attributed to Barlaam as reported by his opponents; not adjudicated.

Condemned at the Constantinople synod of 1341 and later anathematized with his followers at the synods of 1347 and 1351; in Byzantine polemic 'Barlaamite' named the anti-Palamite party. Recorded as historical fact without endorsing either side of the dispute.

Before his defeat in the hesychast controversy Barlaam wrote against the Latin doctrine of the procession of the Holy Spirit (the filioque) and against papal primacy; after 1341 he entered the Latin church and later defended union. His anti-Latin position is attributed to him. Dangling forward reference; filioque is not yet a separate entry.

sources.citation: Meyendorff, John. A Study of Gregory Palamas. Translated by George Lawrence. 2nd ed. Crestwood, NY: St Vladimir's Seminary Press, 1974. The standard academic monograph on Palamas, the hesychast controversy, and the synods of 1341, 1347, and 1351; it treats Barlaam's role, his attack on the hesychasts, and his reported epistemology of God as the principal opponent of Palamas. Academic history-of-doctrine lens; same source and rating as in the gregory-palamas entry.
